# R5 Digest — Seven Trumpets (Rev 8:2–11:19)

**Source:** Grant R. Osborne, *Revelation*, BECNT (Baker, 2002)  
**Slice:** `.cache/osborne-revelation-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R5_trumpets_3645-4507.txt`  
**Declared range:** III.A Seven trumpets 8:2–11:19 (censer intro; trumpets 1–6; interlude little scroll + two witnesses; seventh trumpet)  
**Extractor rules:** Faithfulness only; quote + locus; surveys attributed; no wiki edits; no invented content.

---

## Claims

### C1 — Trumpets as content of the scroll; relation to seals and bowls
Osborne states that the content of the scroll is unveiled in the trumpets and bowls; the trumpet judgments form the middle of the three septets but are more closely related in style and substance to the bowl judgments. The seals are preliminary judgments exploring human depravity and demonstrating the necessity of judgment; saints are sealed from God’s wrath and the judgments themselves but face the wrath of the earth-dwellers.
- **Locus:** intro to 8:2–11:19 (slice ¶ after “3. Seven Trumpets”)
- **Quote:** “The content of the scroll is now unveiled in the trumpets and bowls. The trumpet judgments form the middle of the three septets but are more closely related in style and substance to the bowl judgments. The seals are preliminary judgments that explore the depravity of humankind and demonstrate the necessity of judgment.”

### C2 — Silence, censer, and imprecatory prayers
The silence in heaven is an expectant hush awaiting God’s action—not mere wrath but God’s answer to the imprecatory prayers of the saints (6:9–11 recapitulated in 8:3–4). Worship (golden censer with incense) stands behind the justice.
- **Locus:** intro to 8:2–11:19
- **Quote:** “The silence in heaven is an expectant hush awaiting the action of God, but that is not to be just an outpouring of wrath but God’s answer to the imprecatory prayers of the saints (6:9–11 recapitulated in 8:3–4). Thus there is worship (the golden censer with incense) behind the justice.”

### C3 — Trumpets directed at idolatry; Egyptian plague + Sinai typology
Trumpets (and bowls) address idolatry; first four trumpets recapitulate the Egyptian plagues (Exod. 7–10), themselves addressed to Egyptian gods. Plagues’ threefold purpose: prove Yahweh’s power; show Egyptian gods’ powerlessness; show Pharaoh he could not win—transformed so the third element shows earth-dwellers that Satan cannot win. Michaels (1997: 122) noted (survey): plague imagery transformed by Sinai elements (fire not hail/blood; waters “bitter” reversing Marah; partial dimming closer to Sinai than total plague darkness).
- **Locus:** intro to 8:2–11:19
- **Quote:** “the trumpets are directed at the idolatry so prevalent in John’s day… The first four trumpets recapitulate the Egyptian plagues (Exod. 7–10)… Michaels (1997: 122) notes that the plague imagery has been transformed by adding elements from Sinai.”

### C4 — Structure 4+2+1, woes linking last three, repentance call
Like seals, trumpets take form 4 + 2 + 1 with extensive interlude (10:1–11:13) between sixth and seventh. Last three linked by “woe” sayings (8:13; 9:12; 11:14). Fifth and sixth introduce call to repentance; trumpets participate in the book’s mission—final proof of God’s power and final chance to repent. Court (1979: 79) and Friedrich (TDNT 7:87) attributed for prophetic plague/repentance framing. In 9:20–21 the call is rejected (total depravity stress); in 11:13 some seem to respond and “give glory to God.”
- **Locus:** intro to 8:2–11:19
- **Quote:** “Like the seals, the trumpet judgments take the form of 4 + 2 + 1, with an extensive interlude (10:1–11:13) between the sixth and seventh trumpets. Yet the last three are also linked closely together by the ‘woe’ sayings… In this way the trumpets participate in the mission to the world in the book… In 9:20–21 this call is rejected… but in 11:13… there seem to be a few who respond and ‘give glory to God.’”

### C5 — Trumpets vs bowls: order similar; intensity third vs whole
Building on Roloff’s parallel (1993: 103–4), first four of each affect earth, oceanic waters, inland waters, heavenly bodies, but judgments do not tightly correspond. Uniform intensification: trumpets affect a third of the earth; bowls the whole earth. Only second and third roughly agree in type of judgment, with major differences of execution. Osborne rejects Roloff’s “differing traditions” explanation in favor of distinct visions/images, each producing an indelible image of sovereign power while forming a unity. Krodel (1989: 192) attributed: catastrophes are signs of God’s coming in judgment and salvation, not absence.
- **Locus:** intro; chart Trumpet Cycle / Bowl Cycle
- **Quote:** “there is a uniform intensification in which the trumpets affect a third of the earth and the bowls the whole earth… total uniformity would defeat the purpose of these judgments… Yet they also form a distinct unity focusing on the sovereign power of God.”

### C6 — Chiastic pattern 8:2–6; throne room + heavenly temple; worship produces judgment
Talbert (1994: 38) attributed for chiastic pattern A–B–B′–A′ in 8:2–6 (angels given trumpets; censer with prayers; censer hurled; angels prepare). Jewish apocalyptic metaphors of throne room and heavenly temple both used; altar before the throne (8:3). Worship produces judgment as well as joy because love and justice are interdependent; prayers for justice produce judgments in God’s time (6:11).
- **Locus:** a. Introduction 8:2–6
- **Quote:** “there is a chiastic pattern in verses 2–6… worship throughout this book produces judgment as well as joy… Here the prayers of the saints for justice are brought before God and produce the judgments.”

### C7 — Seven angels as archangels; trumpets as heralds of eschatological judgment
Article on “the seven angels who stand before God” likely points to seven archangels of apocalyptic tradition (Tob. 12:15; 1 Enoch 20.2–8 names). Trumpets make them royal heralds; OT/NT and Jewish uses surveyed (war, temple, enthronement, repentance call, Sinai, day of Yahweh, Matt. 24:31; 1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16). In Revelation: eschatological promise (1:10; 4:1) and harbingers of judgment (these seven).
- **Locus:** 8:2 exegesis
- **Quote:** “it is likely that these are the seven archangels of apocalyptic tradition… These angels are given… seven trumpets, which turn them into royal heralds of the actions of the King of kings.”

### C8 — Angel with golden censer not Christ; one blended altar; incense for prayers
“Another angel” is not Christ (contra Seiss, Walvoord, Beale survey); priestly angelic function. One heavenly altar blends burnt offering (primary 6:9) and incense (primary 8:3–5); Charles (1920: 1.227) attributed—no two altars in ancient Jewish heavenly literature. Incense more likely bears prayers up (dative of advantage “on behalf of”) than identical with them (contra Bruce, Mounce who argue identity via 5:8). Prayers emphasize imprecatory prayers of 6:9–11 within “all the saints” / great multitude of 7:9.
- **Locus:** 8:3–4
- **Quote:** “some believe this is Christ… However… this is another such instance [of priestly angels]… the altar in heaven blends together the altar of burnt offering… and the altar of incense… it is more likely that the incense bore the prayers of the saints up to God.”

### C9 — Censer fire hurled to earth initiates trumpets as vindication (Ezek. 10)
Priestly angel becomes avenging angel; fire from altar hurled to earth (violent “threw,” not Ezek. 10:2’s scattering). Major thrust: fiery judgments are God’s response to the cries of his people and vindication of sufferers (contra Beale 1999: 457–58, last judgment). Second storm theophany of book (after 4:5); first of three after seventh seal/trumpet/bowl (8:5; 11:19; 16:18). Earthquake present in latter three as judgment motif.
- **Locus:** 8:5
- **Quote:** “The major thrust is that the fiery judgments that are to ensue in following chapters are God’s response to the cries of his people and his vindication of his followers for all that they have suffered… this is the first of three further occurrences, each one following the seventh of the seals… trumpets… and bowls…”

### C10 — First four trumpets: idolatry, partial destruction, same 4+2+1 as seals
Purpose of first four: disprove earthly gods, prove sovereignty, last chance for repentance. Each judgment “hurled” like 8:5. Trumpets intensify seals (third of earth) and are intensified by bowls (whole earth). Bowls have 4+3 organization; trumpets share seals’ 4+2+1; seventh symbolizes eschaton.
- **Locus:** b. First Four Trumpets 8:7–12 intro + Summary
- **Quote:** “the trumpets have the same 4 + 2 + 1 organization as the seals (the bowls have a 4 + 3 organization)… The trumpet judgments intensify the seals, affecting a third of the earth, and are intensified in turn by the bowls that affect the whole earth.”

### C11 — First trumpet (8:7): seventh Egyptian plague + Joel; “all” grass; apocalyptic non-harmonization
Hail and fire mixed with blood: Exod. 9 seventh plague plus Joel 2:30–31 fire/blood; final fulfillment of day of Yahweh. Contemporary Aegean volcanic parallels not ruled out (Osborne). A third of earth/trees burned; all green grass burned—for apocalyptic effect. Contradiction with 9:4 (“do not harm the grass”) not to be harmonized: “another apocalyptic image… not supposed to be harmonized”; cyclical nature allows seeming contradictions.
- **Locus:** 8:7
- **Quote:** “It is best to see this as another apocalyptic image that is not supposed to be harmonized but taken as is. The cyclical nature of these judgments allows for such seeming contradictions… Each vision is a self-contained unit in this sense.”

### C12 — Second trumpet (8:8–9): burning mountain into sea; partial blood; repentance space
“Like a huge mountain blazing with fire” cast into sea; sources surveyed without exclusive choice: Jer. 51:25 Babylon; 1 Enoch / Sib. Or. 5; Vesuvius/Aegean volcanoes; meteorite (Artemis of Ephesus). Third of sea blood, sea life, ships destroyed—more devastating than first Egyptian plague for sea-dependent Rome; still partial, allowing repentance.
- **Locus:** 8:8–9
- **Quote:** “Still, it is a partial judgment, allowing time for repentance. If the nations will realize the message and turn from their earthly gods to the one living and true God, there is still time to repent.”

### C13 — Third trumpet (8:10–11): Wormwood; bitter waters; reverse Marah
Huge star blazing like a torch (= meteorite, not fallen angel of 9:1). Named Wormwood; third of fresh waters bitter; many die. Poisonous water as divine judgment (Deut./Jer.); often seen as reversal of Marah (Exod. 15:23)—parallel obvious but hard to prove John intended it. Springs as life metaphor reversed to death.
- **Locus:** 8:10–11
- **Quote:** “It is also common to see here a reversal of the miracle of Marah (Exod. 15:23)… The parallel is obvious, though it is difficult to prove that John had this in mind.”

### C14 — Fourth trumpet (8:12): partial cosmic darkness; prepares fifth bowl
Replicates ninth Egyptian plague but partial (third of day/night); every luminary named for emphasis; total darkness for that third, not mere eclipse. Darkness as eschatological judgment (Joel, Amos, Mark 13, etc.). Prepares for fifth bowl darkening of beast’s kingdom (16:10).
- **Locus:** 8:12
- **Quote:** “this plague is partial, affecting only one-third of the day and night… The darkness here prepares for the fifth bowl, where the kingdom of the beast is ‘darkened’…”

### C15 — Beale’s “third” from Ezek. 5 rejected
Additional note: Beale (1999: 476) links “third” to Ezek. 5:2, 12 (famine fulfillment). Osborne: too little connection with Ezek. 5; no hint famine is intended.
- **Locus:** Additional Notes 8:7
- **Quote:** “there is too little connection with Ezek. 5 here and no hint that famine is intended in this judgment.”

### C16 — Woes intro (8:13): eagle/vulture; threefold woe; earth-dwellers
Last three trumpets unique among septets in being preceded by prophetic woe warnings. Eagle (or vulture) flying midair announces “Woe! Woe! Woe to the inhabitants of the earth.” Threefold woe obverse of “holy, holy, holy” (4:8); holiness demands judgment. Midair links 14:6 eternal gospel and 19:17 carrion birds—choice of two fates. Earth-dwellers = followers of beast who oppose/kill saints; objects of wrath.
- **Locus:** c. Fifth Trumpet intro; 8:13
- **Quote:** “The last three trumpets are unique in the three septets in that they are preceded by prophetic warnings of woe… the primary thrust is… a portent of death and destruction… his holiness demands his judgment.”

### C17 — Fifth/sixth trumpets prove demonic hatred; torture then kill; still no repentance
Ch. 9 judgments three times as long as first four combined. Prove false gods are demonic and hate their worshipers (Gospel possession pattern: torture and kill). Locusts torture five months (long for death); horsemen kill a third. Despite proof of God’s power and demonic hatred, people refuse to repent (9:20–21).
- **Locus:** intro to 8:13–9:11
- **Quote:** “In spite of absolute proof of both the omnipotence of God and the hatred of the false gods for their own followers, evil people do not repent but reject God’s offer and return again to worship the very evil powers that had just tortured and killed so many of them (9:20–21).”

### C18 — Star-angel of 9:1 is good messenger, not Satan; key to abyss
Survey: many take fallen star as demon/Satan (Kiddle, Walvoord, Beale et al.). Osborne: only place God would use evil angel; Thompson notes fallen angel shouldn’t hold key to own prison; parallel 20:1 descending angel with key; third trumpet falling star not angelic. Star-angel is divine messenger; edothē stresses sovereignty. Abyss = prison of fallen angels / place of dead; closed prison (smoke, beast emerges, Satan bound 20:1–3).
- **Locus:** 9:1
- **Quote:** “this would be the only place in Revelation where God used an evil angel to execute his will… Therefore, this was another of the angelic messengers sent from heaven to do God’s will.”

### C19 — Locusts from abyss: Joel + eighth plague; sealed exempt; five months limit
Locusts reenact Joel 1–2 and Exod. 10; demons in guise of locusts (Aune). Given power like scorpions; cannot harm vegetation—only those without seal of God (7:3–4; parallel Exod. protection of Israel). Cannot kill, only torment five months (locust lifespan/dry season background; main point: strict divine time limit, possibly for repentance). Seek death but death flees—lex talionis irony after they killed martyrs.
- **Locus:** 9:2–6
- **Quote:** “Only those who have rejected his call to repentance (9:20–21) are subject to judgment… The main point is that God has placed a strict time limit on the torture, possibly to give the people time to repent (9:20–21)… There is a certain irony in that they have killed the martyrs of 6:9–11, but God will not let them die.”

### C20 — Locust description (9:7–10): Joel war imagery; crowns “like” gold (usurpers)
Appearance combines locust, scorpion, invading army; Joel 1:6–7; 2:4–5. Crowns “resembling gold” not true gold crowns of celestial beings—usurper’s crown; earthly authority only. Tails with stings; five-month injury restated: demons seek torture then kill; God allows short period so people realize fruit of following Satan and may repent/glorify God (11:13; 14:7).
- **Locus:** 9:7–10
- **Quote:** “the ‘goldlike crown’ here is a usurper’s crown… from God’s standpoint, this is a short period during which the people of earth are given a chance to realize the fruit of following Satan, then repent and ‘glorify God’ (11:13; 14:7).”

### C21 — King Abaddon/Apollyon (9:11): destroyer; possible Apollo/Domitian side point
King over them = angel of the abyss (not same as key-angel of 9:1; more likely chief lieutenant than Satan, though Aune argues Satan). Hebrew Abaddon / Greek Apollyon = Destroyer; irony destroyer soon destroyed. Possible side allusion: Apollo (pestilence; locust symbol) and Domitian as Apollo incarnate—imperial cult tip, not main point. Real message: demonic organization, hatred for followers.
- **Locus:** 9:11; Summary
- **Quote:** “The real message is that the demonic forces are organized, powerful, terrifying, and filled with hatred and contempt for their followers… demonic powers are behind all idolatry, and their purpose is to destroy rather than to build up.”

### C22 — Sixth trumpet (9:12–21): from torture to death; intensifies seals; depravity
Second woe completes first: third of humankind dies. Organization parallels fifth (release then description). Connected to fourth seal (¼ killed by sword/famine/plague, 6:8)—intensifies results and process: demonic war on humans not human-on-human. Mounce (1998: 193) attributed for portrait of sinful humanity pressed to extreme—greater punishment, increased rebellion.
- **Locus:** d. Sixth Trumpet intro
- **Quote:** “The effect of the seals was the death of a quarter of the population; now this intensifies to a third… people will still reject the God of the universe and refuse to repent.”

### C23 — Voice from golden altar; four bound angels at Euphrates; prepared time; 200 million
Voice from horns of golden altar (likely angel of 8:3–5, not God; divine imprimatur; response to saints’ prayers). Sixth trumpet angel told to release four angels bound at Euphrates—“bound” favors demonic; leaders of cavalry. Euphrates: eastern Roman boundary, Parthian dread, OT invasion symbol; prepares sixth bowl (16:12). Prepared “for this hour and day and month and year” (divine passive; exact eschatological moment). Purpose: kill a third of humankind; saints protected. Cavalry 200 million (2× myriads of myriads); “I heard their number” / “I saw in my vision” stress prophetic reception not literary invention.
- **Locus:** 9:13–16
- **Quote:** “this terrible judgment again is God’s response to the prayers of the saints (6:10)… these angels had been… made ready… by God ‘for this very hour and day and month and year’… to ‘kill a third of humankind’… As before, the purpose even of such mass destruction is redemptive.”

### C24 — Demonic cavalry description (9:17–19): fire, smoke, sulfur; mouths and snake tails
Breastplates fiery red, dusky blue, sulfurous yellow = colors of fire/smoke/sulfur from mouths. Lion heads; three plagues (not modern weapons). Power in mouths (kill) and tails like snakes (injure)—Satan “ancient serpent”; Luke 10:19 reversed. Parody of sword from Christ’s mouth; irony of breathing own future torment (19:20; 20:10).
- **Locus:** 9:17–19
- **Quote:** “there is great irony in the demonic forces breathing out the same ‘fire, smoke, and sulfur’ that will become their own eternal torment… This is another of the dominant themes of the book, the imitation of the work of God and the Lamb by the dragon, the beast, and their demonic hordes.”

### C25 — Refusal to repent (9:20–21): idolatry = demon worship; vice list; final offer
“Rest of humankind” refuse to repent of works of hands = idols (gold, silver, bronze, wood, stone—lifeless, Ps. 115 echo) yet worship demons behind them (Deut. 32; 1 Cor. 10:20). Vice list: murders, magic arts (pharmakon—potions/paraphernalia not just general sorcery), immorality, thefts—echo Ten Commandments + Nicolaitan vices. Call to repent for unbelievers outside letters only 9:20–21; 16:9, 11. Purpose of seals/trumpets/bowls: final offer of salvation (contra Beale, Aune, Schnabel) and demonstrate depravity. “These plagues” most likely the three of 9:18 (plēgē first appears there).
- **Locus:** 9:20–21
- **Quote:** “This is one of the purposes of the seals, trumpets, and bowls—to give a final offer of salvation to the nations (contra Beale, Aune, Schnabel) and to demonstrate the depravity of a people who would reject it… rather than turn to the God of mercy, the unbelievers turn once more to their idols…”

### C26 — Theodicy and mission after 9:20–21; not timetable
Fifth/sixth show theodicy: justifying redemptive love and justice of judgments (Osborne 1993: 63–77). Modern idols (money, power, sex, etc.) parallel. Not apocalyptic timetable for John’s day or ours—wrong to equate Parthians/Vesuvius or helicopters/tanks; symbolic depictions of future events with theological messages for present.
- **Locus:** Summary 9:12–21
- **Quote:** “Thus we see once more the theodicy of the book, justifying the redemptive love of God and the justice of his judgments… John’s purpose is not to give an apocalyptic timetable… These are symbolic depictions of future events but with theological messages for the present…”

### C27 — Interlude 10:1–11:13: prophecy motif; little scroll; mission after failed limited judgments
Like ch. 7, interlude clarifies saints’ role; two parts: little scroll (10:1–11) and two witnesses (11:1–13) with measuring narrative (11:1–2). Prophecy terms cluster (10:7, 11; 11:3, 6, 10; cf. 11:18). John recommissioned to “prophesy again” (back to 1:19). Scroll of chs. 5 and 10 one and the same (debated). Bauckham (1993b: 257–58) attributed four preparatory themes; limited judgments of seals/trumpets failed to bring repentance (9:20–21), so scroll provides “more effective strategy”—conversion of nations; many converted only in 11:13b. Saints protected from God’s wrath not beast’s (11:7; 13:7); martyrdom is victory (12:11). Introduces 42 months / 1,260 days and “beast.”
- **Locus:** e. Interlude intro
- **Quote:** “Since the limited judgments of the seals and trumpets failed to bring humankind to repentance (9:20–21), the scroll will provide ‘a more effective strategy’ for reaching the world… Many are converted in 11:13b, the only place in the book where this occurs… Christians are protected from God’s wrath but not from the beast’s wrath.”

### C28 — Mighty angel 10:1–4: not Christ; little scroll open; seven thunders sealed
“Another mighty angel” (not same as 5:2; not Christ despite parallels—Beale’s angelomorphic case surveyed and rejected as primary; “angelic representative of Christ” more likely). Description: cloud, rainbow, face like sun, legs like fiery pillars—glory, mercy, deliverance (Exod. pillar). Biblaridion open: identity with ch. 5 scroll but not absolute unity—small portion of whole plan re: church’s place; sweet/bitter for people of God; 11:1–13 witnessing. Feet on sea and land = dominion (Colossus of Rhodes popular myth background). Seven thunders (Ps. 29) speak; John forbidden to write—seal. Survey of thunder interpretations; Osborne: general judgment from Ps. 29; sphragison = Dan. 12:4 seal + ch. 5 sovereign ownership; message: God in control; saints need not know all details.
- **Locus:** 10:1–4
- **Quote:** “There is identity between the two scrolls but not absolute unity… The scroll here is a ‘small’ portion of the whole scroll… depicting the place of the church in these events… The major message is one of sovereignty. God is in control, and the saints do not need to know all the details.”

### C29 — Angel’s oath 10:5–7: no more delay; mystery completed at seventh trumpet
Dan. 12:7 parallel; answers martyrs’ “how long” (6:10). “There will be no more delay”—eschaton predicted by Daniel has arrived; tribulation time designations begin after ch. 10. In days of seventh angel’s voice, when he must sound, “the mystery of God will be brought to completion” as announced to slaves the prophets (Amos 3:7 with euēngelisen “good news”). “Days” plural: not only parousia but day-of-Yahweh events (likely chs. 19–21 given seventh trumpet at end of history). “No more delay” does not mean immediate return but no delay of events inaugurating return.
- **Locus:** 10:5–7; intro to 10:1–11
- **Quote:** “‘There will be no more delay!’… the time of the eschaton predicted by Daniel has now arrived… when he must sound the seventh trumpet, the mystery of God will be brought to completion… ‘no more delay’ does not mean Christ’s return will occur immediately but rather there will be ‘no delay’ in the events that will inaugurate that return.”

### C30 — Eating the scroll 10:8–11: Ezekiel commission; sweet/bitter for church; prophesy about nations
Voice from heaven: take and eat—Ezek. 2:8–3:3. Sweet as honey / bitter in stomach: not limited to John; sweet = sovereign will, vindication, reward; bitter = suffering, persecution, martyrdom. Commission: “You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.” Epi surveyed “about” vs “against”—both warning and witness; negative warning predominates in seals/trumpets/bowls context; only list with “many” and “kings.”
- **Locus:** 10:8–11; Summary
- **Quote:** “It is ‘sweet’ because God’s sovereign will is always for the benefit of his people… It is ‘bitter’ because it will involve great suffering and persecution, even martyrdom… the prophetic activity to which John is called contains both emphases, though probably with negative warning predominating…”

### C31 — Measuring temple 11:1–2: spiritual protection; outer court trampled 42 months
Prophetic action paralleling Ezek. 40–42 / Zech. 2: measure temple, altar, worshipers = ownership and spiritual protection of church (heavenly-temple imagery, not literal rebuilt temple—contra dispensational Seiss/Walvoord/Thomas). Exclude outer court given to Gentiles who trample Holy City 42 months—church handed over for persecution; physical harm allowed, spiritual harm not. Holy City also symbolizes people of God. Forty-two months = Dan. 7:25 etc. three-and-a-half years; also Elijah drought / wilderness encampments; limited tribulation under God’s control; time of church (martyrdom + preservation + witness). Parallel sealing of 7:1–8.
- **Locus:** 11:1–2
- **Quote:** “God will protect his people not from physical harm but rather from spiritual harm… the ‘outer court’ is unprotected, for God will allow the pagans to ‘trample’ the saints for the period of the ‘great tribulation’… The powers of evil can ‘conquer’ them in a physical sense (13:7), but Satan will be ‘conquered’ by them in the more important spiritual sense (12:11).”

### C32 — Two witnesses identity: individuals (Moses/Elijah-like) and symbol of church
Hotly contested. Historical individuals at end of history “in spirit and power” of Moses and Elijah (not themselves; not Law/Prophets as such); beast individual (11:7; 13:1) supports individuals. Simultaneously symbol of witnessing church (Beale’s six reasons accepted for corporate function). Ladd (1972: 154) blending of symbolic and specific—Osborne’s position.
- **Locus:** 11:3–13 intro
- **Quote:** “I believe it is likely the witnesses will be historical figures… like the Baptist… they will appear ‘in the spirit and power’ of Moses and Elijah… At the same time, the context of this interlude… makes it probable that they do stand for the witnessing church… Ladd… ‘a blending of the symbolic and specific.’”

### C33 — Witnesses’ ministry 11:3–6: 1,260 days; sackcloth; Zech. 4; Elijah/Moses plagues
God “I will give” authority (contrast 11:2 give to Gentiles). Two witnesses for Deuteronomic legal requirement. Prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth—mourning and call to repentance. Two olive trees and two lampstands (Zech. 4 reworked)—Spirit/eyes of Lord; priestly and kingly roles of church. Fire from mouth (Elijah vs Ahaziah; also proclamation of judgment / sword-from-mouth parallel). Shut heavens (Elijah drought = 1,260 days); waters to blood and every plague (Moses/Egypt)—prove earthly gods powerless; executors of divine judgments transforming trumpet theme (Michaels).
- **Locus:** 11:3–6
- **Quote:** “the two witnesses/people of God become the ‘executors of divine judgments’… these prove that the demonic forces and the earthly gods have no power, and Yahweh alone controls the natural forces.”

### C34 — Death by beast 11:7–10: Dan. 7; great city Jerusalem-Rome; earth-dwellers rejoice
When testimony complete, beast from abyss wages war, conquers, kills (Dan. 7:7–21 language; same as 13:7—only by God’s allowance). Corpse in street of “great city” spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where Lord crucified—Jerusalem in context yet amalgam with Rome as Antichrist capital; secondary every self-sufficient city. Unburied three and a half days (short vs 1,260); peoples/tribes/languages/nations watch; earth-dwellers rejoice, send gifts—because prophets “tormented” them (lex talionis harbinger of final torment).
- **Locus:** 11:7–10
- **Quote:** “Jerusalem and Rome are combined into a single, symbolic ‘great city,’ the capital of the new ‘unholy Roman Empire’ headed by the Antichrist… The familiar Christian ‘gospel,’ the story of suffering and death followed by vindication… is what transforms the ending of the trumpet series from nonrepentance (9:20–21) to repentance (11:13).” (Michaels 1997: 141 attributed in body)

### C35 — Resurrection 11:11–12: Ezek. 37; cloud ascension; proleptic of church rapture
Breath of life from God; stand on feet (Ezek. 37). Great fear. Loud voice “Come up here”; ascend in cloud—vindication through resurrection/rapture imagery, not primarily prophetic commissioning (contra Beale on 4:1 parallel alone). Timing: after 3½ years but before full parousia sequence—proleptic anticipation of church rapture, not the rapture itself. Enemies watch (theōreō may prelude faith as in John).
- **Locus:** 11:11–12
- **Quote:** “it seems more likely that the resurrection of the witnesses is a proleptic anticipation of the ‘rapture’ of the church rather than being the ‘rapture’ itself.”

### C36 — Earthquake and true repentance 11:13: partial judgment; not universalism
Great earthquake; tenth of city falls; 7,000 killed (reverse of 1 Kgs 19:18 reserved seven thousand). Survivors terrified and “gave glory to the God of heaven”—true repentance/conversion (majority of scholars named; 14:6–7; 15:4; 16:9 support), not forced homage (contra Hendriksen, Kiddle, Mounce, Beale, Schnabel survey). Not universalism: city’s portion, not all earth-dwellers; death of witnesses alone not cause—resurrection + earthquake; final judgment still critical in rest of book. Portion of earth-dwellers from every nation repent.
- **Locus:** 11:13; Additional Note on Jewish conversion rejected
- **Quote:** “giving glory to God is clearly the consequence of repentance, i.e., conversion… This refers to a portion of the earth-dwellers who repent rather than symbolizing the repentance of all the unbelievers… Here we have the response of some, and it is a critical message… Their suffering in reality is their triumph, and God will use that suffering to bring people to himself.”

### C37 — Seventh trumpet = third woe content; eschaton celebrated, not deferred
Third woe is 11:15–19 itself (judgment proclaimed not described; aorists look back on completion)—not deferred to chs. 12–13, bowls, or 12–20. Confirmed by 10:7 mystery completed at seventh trumpet. Concludes major section 4:1–11:19; inclusio with elders from chs. 4–5; sets stage for rest of book. Second woe finalized only after interlude completes picture of saints during first two woes.
- **Locus:** f. Seventh Trumpet intro; 11:14
- **Quote:** “Those who say that 11:15–19 do indeed form the content of the third woe… are more likely correct… the judgment of the third woe is proclaimed rather than described… We must note 10:7: ‘the mystery of God will be brought to completion’ at the sounding of the seventh trumpet… Here once more we are at the eschaton, further proof of the cyclical nature of the seals, trumpets, and bowls.”

### C38 — Kingdom hymn 11:15: world kingdom becomes Lord’s and Messiah’s
Loud voices in heaven (plural unique): “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Messiah, and he will reign forever and ever.” Aorists proleptic/certitude. Oneness of God and Christ; messianic office. Fulfills Dan. 7:13–14 everlasting dominion; Ps. 2:2 opposition reversed.
- **Locus:** 11:15
- **Quote:** “the turning point that the entire Bible has waited for—the arrival of the kingdom!… at the eschaton the heavenly kingdom will be the only reality… The temporal reign of sin… will be replaced by an eternal Godhead, an eternal kingdom, and eternal life…”

### C39 — Elders’ thanksgiving 11:16–18: “who is and who was” (no “is to come”); chiasm of judgment/reward
Elders fall and worship; only eucharistoumen in book. Title “Lord God Almighty”; threefold formula omits “who is to come”—no more future; eschaton arrived (Beale: replaced by hoti clause of taking power). Taken great power and begun to reign—day of the Lord content of seventh trumpet (chs. 18–22 described later). Ps. 2: nations angry / your wrath came. Chiasm: judge dead // reward slaves-prophets-saints-fearers small and great // destroy destroyers of earth (= Babylon/beast followers; Jer. 51:25). Prophets and saints two groups both “slaves”; not three; not whole church as “prophets.”
- **Locus:** 11:16–18
- **Quote:** “the most significant change of the threefold formula occurs here… for ὁ ἐρχόμενος… has been omitted. There is no more future, for God’s awesome power has acted, and his eternal reign has begun. We are at the eschaton!… ‘and your wrath has come, namely the time for the dead to be judged… and to give a reward… and to destroy those who destroy the earth.’”

### C40 — Temple opened; ark appears; storm theophany 11:19
Temple of God in heaven opened; ark of covenant appears—closest to theophany in chs. 1–19; mercy (ark) and judgment (storm). Inclusio with measuring 11:1–2. Heavenly ark pattern of earthly; Jewish traditions of hidden ark awaiting end part of background. Storm theophany third of four (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18–21)—Sinai majesty + eschaton; great hail intensifies (Exod. 9; Ezek. 38; Josh. 10). Links to 21:3 God dwelling with people. Ōphthē also 12:1, 3—linear movement into ch. 12.
- **Locus:** 11:19; Summary
- **Quote:** “This is the closest we come in chapters 1–19 to a theophany… God is present in mercy (the ark) and judgment (the storm theophany)… Finally, at the last trumpet… the temple of heaven will be opened, and the ark of the covenant will be revealed. God will live among his people…”

### C41 — First four trumpets’ purpose summary (material, sea trade, light)
Together prove living only for this world is foolish; only in God is true life. First: material world no answer; second/third: sea trade/food; fourth: celestial heat and light for life itself.
- **Locus:** Summary 8:7–12
- **Quote:** “The purpose of the first four trumpet judgments is primarily to disprove the earthly gods and to show that Yahweh alone is on the throne… The four together prove that those who live only for this world have chosen foolishly, for only in God is there true life.”

### C42 — Hermeneutical stance on ch. 9: primarily futurist tribulation; secondary idealist/preterist
Fifth/sixth primarily what God will do just before eschaton; secondary significance for John’s church and today. Idealist pure symbolism of inter-advent Satan activity rejected as sole frame; literal event whose exact historical working-out God has not fully specified—“We will have to wait and see.”
- **Locus:** Additional Notes 9:11; Summary 9:1–11
- **Quote:** “I interpret this primarily as a reference to demonic activity in the last epoch of world history (commonly understood as the ‘tribulation period’) but with secondary significance for the church of John’s day and the church today… This is a literal event, but how literal it will be is up to God…”
